# HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvement for Harness Token Efficiency

Yuhua Jiang
Email: <mailto:yh-jiang24@mails.tsinghua.edu.cnblackyh-jiang24@mails.tsinghua.edu.cnmailto:chanx@microsoft.comblackchanx@microsoft.com>
   Chang Xu Affiliation: Tsinghua University Microsoft Research Asia
(MSRA)
Email: <mailto:feifiegao@tsinghua.edu.cnblackfeifiegao@tsinghua.edu.cnmailto:lizo@microsoft.comblacklizo@microsoft.com>
   Feifei Gao    Li Zhao Affiliation: Tsinghua University Microsoft
Research Asia (MSRA)

###### Abstract

Agent harnesses repeatedly invoke reasoning after tool feedback, even
when an earlier call has already fixed the next action. We introduce
HarnessMM (Harness Minus Minus), a method for improving harness token
efficiency through guarded decision reuse and recursive self-improvement
(RSI). RSI iteratively refines companion harness configurations from
training feedback, with validation selecting the configuration for
deployment. A controller at the model–tool boundary reuses resolved
decisions to replace later reasoning callbacks while actor weights
remain fixed. Executable Decision Graphs store exact actions, literal
arguments, causal dependencies and public guards. Guarded Decision Reuse
activates these persistent decisions from observed receipts; Certified
Callback Substitution executes them through the native interface and
records removal of the registered slow callback. New semantic decisions,
unsupported evidence and selector abstention invoke the original actor
again. The representation restricts what feedback may change, while
complete-task measurements establish quality and cost. On HumanEval,
HarnessMM preserves Codex success at 90.82% while reducing Tokens/task
(k) from 66.72 to 47.02 (29.54% saving). For DeepSeek Harness, success
rises from 71.43% to 85.71% while Tokens/task (k) fall from 96.28 to
11.62 (87.93% saving). A separate MBPP ablation measures 26.91% lower
cost than single-use graphs and 19.52% lower cost than retained
callbacks. These results establish guarded decision reuse as a practical
way to reduce repeated reasoning in existing harnesses.

![Refer to caption](2610.32813v1/figures/harness_rsi_overview_user.png)

Figure 1: HarnessMM overview. The upper row shows RSI updating a harness

## 1 Introduction

Agent harnesses connect model reasoning to tool execution. ReAct
alternates reasoning, actions and observations \[[46](#bib.bib46)\];
SWE-agent demonstrates that interface design shapes software-engineering
performance \[[44](#bib.bib47)\], and Toolformer learns when to call
APIs \[[33](#bib.bib48)\]. After each tool result, the harness must
decide whether the observation demands new reasoning or merely permits
an already resolved action to execute. Repeated deliberation can
regenerate decisions whose semantics have not changed.

Efficiency methods intervene at different points. Prompt compression and
history management reduce the input replayed into a
call \[[16](#bib.bib15), [17](#bib.bib16), [30](#bib.bib17),
[42](#bib.bib33), [21](#bib.bib34)\]. Fast–slow architectures and
routing change who reasons and how deeply \[[4](#bib.bib43),
[45](#bib.bib44), [27](#bib.bib51)\]. Executable skills,
observation-independent plans and compiled tool dependencies reuse or
schedule prior computation \[[40](#bib.bib19), [43](#bib.bib49),
[19](#bib.bib50)\]. ActionEngine further executes task programs against
reusable application memory with reactive repair \[[52](#bib.bib54)\].
These methods already establish the value of programmatic execution.
HarnessMM studies a narrower contract: an episode-specific action
remains literal, later feedback changes its eligibility, and the
execution record identifies the reasoning boundary actually bypassed.

Feedback can optimize instructions and agent programs through APE, STOP,
ADAS, Self-Refine and Reflexion \[[53](#bib.bib18), [49](#bib.bib25),
[13](#bib.bib26), [24](#bib.bib52), [36](#bib.bib53)\]. Such
optimization constructs a harness; its deployment still determines which
callbacks recur. Jev’s typed probability interface \[[1](#bib.bib3)\]
motivates compact candidate selection, but adding a selector does not
remove the original callback automatically. We call this accounting
mismatch the _Substitution Paradox_: computation is saved only when
eliminated reasoning exceeds added authorship, selection and recovery.

A concrete opportunity appears when slow reasoning fixes several actions
before their execution feedback arrives. After writing a program, the
next compilation command can already be specified; after compilation, a
successful return code can activate an already-specified test command.
We call a decision resolved when prior reasoning has fixed its action
and literal arguments; the unknown tool receipt determines whether that
action is ready to execute. The example separates _semantic uncertainty_
from _execution uncertainty_ and suggests a different role for feedback:
activating a resolved decision. Our insight is that such decisions can
persist across feedback boundaries as guarded executable commitments. An
authored graph can serve multiple transitions while its continuations
remain resolved; new inference returns control to the slow actor, which
may reason and author further graphs throughout the task.

We introduce HarnessMM (Harness Minus Minus), a method for improving
harness token efficiency by changing when the harness invokes its
reasoning model
(Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).
HarnessMM inserts a controller at the native decision boundary while
keeping model weights, tools and task interfaces fixed. Executable
Decision Graphs (EDGs) store actions and literal arguments already
resolved by slow reasoning, together with their dependencies and public
execution guards. Guarded Decision Reuse (GDR) retains these decisions
across tool transitions and checks whether observed receipts satisfy
their guards. Certified Callback Substitution (CCS) then dispatches the
stored action through the native interface and omits the corresponding
reasoning callback. A typed selector chooses an eligible decision or
abstains; new semantic decisions, unsupported evidence and abstention
return control to the original actor. This changes the harness’s
execution policy so that resolved actions avoid repeated context input
and reasoning output while unresolved decisions retain access to the
original reasoning process. Complete-task accounting includes graph
authorship, selection, remaining slow calls, fallback and unsuccessful
executions. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) iteratively refines
companion harness configurations: the current harness supplies training
feedback for candidate edits, validation selects the retained candidate,
and that harness supplies the next round’s training feedback. The
selected configuration is frozen before test evaluation
(Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Recorded rule-development protocol ‣ Appendix B Implementation and selection ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).

We integrate HarnessMM into Codex and DeepSeek Harness and evaluate each
against its original harness. On the same 98 HumanEval test tasks,
HarnessMM preserves Codex success at 90.82% while reducing Tokens/task
(k) from 66.72 to 47.02, a 29.54% saving. For DeepSeek Harness, success
rises from 71.43% to 85.71% while Tokens/task (k) fall from 96.28 to
11.62, an 87.93% saving
(Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Industrial harness results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).
These comparisons demonstrate that improving when a harness invokes
reasoning and executes actions can reduce token consumption while
preserving or improving task performance. An MBPP ablation isolates
persistent decision reuse and callback removal, measuring 26.91% lower
cost than single-use graphs and 19.52% lower cost than retained
callbacks. Companion studies evaluate their benchmark-specific
instruction and context configurations separately
(Section [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Companion configurations: quality and cost ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).

Our contributions are:

- •
  EDGs separate resolved action semantics from feedback-dependent
  readiness, making prior deliberation executable at future tool
  boundaries.
- •
  GDR retains the graph and uses public receipts to activate causally
  ordered actions while reserving new decisions for slow reasoning.
- •
  CCS substitutes native execution for registered callbacks and verifies
  omission with receipt-bound certificates. The MBPP ablation measures
  how reuse and callback substitution affect success and complete task
  cost.

## 2 Related Work

##### Prompt, context and reasoning compression.

LLMLingua and its successors compress prompt inputs \[[16](#bib.bib15),
[17](#bib.bib16), [30](#bib.bib17)\]; AgentDiet and observation masking
reduce replayed trajectory context \[[42](#bib.bib33),
[21](#bib.bib34)\]. Thinking budgets control generated
reasoning \[[15](#bib.bib35)\]. These methods reduce the size or depth
of a call; HarnessMM targets whether that call needs to recur at all.

##### Fast–slow agents and model routing.

Talker–Reasoner separates response and planning \[[4](#bib.bib43)\];
CogRouter adapts cognitive depth \[[45](#bib.bib44)\]; boundary-guided
routing chooses the reasoning model \[[50](#bib.bib36)\]. Jev motivates
typed compact decisions \[[1](#bib.bib3)\]. Our Jev-motivated typed
selector uses a candidate-ID/abstention interface, with single-token
decoding when selection requires a model call. HarnessMM studies whether
such a compact decision actually removes a future reasoning callback.

##### Skills, memory and reusable programs.

Chain-of-thought prompting exposes intermediate
reasoning \[[41](#bib.bib38)\], Voyager retains executable
skills \[[40](#bib.bib19)\], and SkillLens retrieves procedural
context \[[25](#bib.bib37)\]. A skill or macro can inform future
reasoning or encapsulate a routine. An EDG instead stores
episode-specific, fully resolved semantic commitments; public execution
conditions control their activation. This distinction allows execution
to replace a reasoning call rather than merely guide it.

##### Agent and harness optimization.

APE, STOP and ADAS improve prompts, programs and agent configurations
from feedback \[[53](#bib.bib18), [49](#bib.bib25), [13](#bib.bib26)\].
Self-modification methods extend the search to improvement
operators \[[47](#bib.bib27), [51](#bib.bib28), [38](#bib.bib24)\].
HarnessMM changes when a harness calls its reasoning model and when it
directly executes a previously resolved action. Instruction
optimization, context compaction and RSI supply companion
configurations; they are outside the core execution method and retain
separate experimental attribution. Their development protocols and costs
appear in
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Recorded rule-development protocol ‣ Appendix B Implementation and selection ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency").

## 3 Problem Formulation

### 3.1 Reasoning calls and tool actions in a harness

The actor parameters $`\theta`$ are fixed. An existing harness $`h`$
supplies instructions, context and native execution rules. HarnessMM
intervenes at its reasoning callbacks: a stored action may replace a new
model call. For task $`x`$, unroll a finite execution under the
benchmark limits into a computation graph $`\mathcal{G}_{h}(x)=(V,E)`$.
Nodes include reasoning, retrieval, routing, tools, verification and
recovery; edges encode execution dependencies. For policy $`\pi`$, node
$`v`$ has model-token cost $`c_{v}`$, giving

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
C(\pi)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{v\in V}\mathbf{1}\{v\text{ invoked under }\pi\}\,c_{v}\right].
``` |  | (1) |

The fast–slow policy changes which reasoning nodes recur after public
feedback. Deterministic tools use no actor tokens but affect subsequent
calls and quality. Both node costs and invocation probabilities can
change when a continuation is substituted. We use $`s_{t}`$ for public
state at transition $`t`$: the request, observed tool feedback and
completed action history.

### 3.2 Capability-constrained computation substitution

Let $`Q_{b}(h)=\mathbb{E}[m_{b}(\operatorname{Run}_{\theta}(x;h))]`$,
where $`m_{b}`$ is benchmark $`b`$’s official score. Relative to the
original harness $`h_{0}`$, define capability regret
$`R_{b}(\pi)=Q_{b}(h_{0})-Q_{b}(h_{\pi})`$. The objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\min_{\pi}C(\pi)\quad\text{subject to}\quad R_{b}(\pi)\leq\epsilon_{b}
``` |  | (2) |

for every declared quality endpoint, equivalently
$`Q_{b}(h_{\pi})\geq Q_{b}(h_{0})-\epsilon_{b}`$. This is a policy-level
constraint, assessed by evaluating both harnesses on the same tasks.
Tolerances are fixed before evaluation; zero-regret protocols use
$`\epsilon_{b}=0`$. Both harnesses are evaluated on the full task set to
assess the constraint, including unsuccessful tasks. The original tools,
evaluator and limits are shared within each comparison. Finite-sample
score differences and uncertainty are reported under the bound protocol
(Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Recorded rule-development protocol ‣ Appendix B Implementation and selection ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).

### 3.3 The Substitution Paradox

The paradox arises when fast–slow composition adds a decision without
removing its downstream deliberation. If a fast stage costs $`C_{f}`$
but removes none of an original continuation’s $`C_{n}`$ tokens, its
additive path costs $`C_{n}+C_{f}`$. Short output alone cannot resolve
this overhead: typed output and frequent fast-path activation do not
establish callback elimination. A beneficial substitution requires

|     |                                               |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       C_{\mathrm{removed}}>C_{\mathrm{introduced}},
       ```                                            |     | (3) |

where introduced computation includes authorship, routing, additional
context and any fallback or recovery. This cost condition and the
capability constraint address separate requirements.

## 4 HarnessMM: Reusing Decisions

HarnessMM changes the route from tool feedback to the next native
action. EDG stores resolved decisions, GDR determines their eligibility,
and CCS substitutes native execution for registered slow callbacks. The
controller integrates with an existing harness through its public-state
adapter, slow-call entry point and native action dispatcher.

##### Method boundary and fixed configuration.

The core method decides whether a stored action can replace the next
reasoning call. Prompt editing, context compaction and finalization
rules configure the surrounding harness. They are developed on training
data, selected before evaluation and held fixed during each run. The
runtime selector chooses an eligible EDG node or abstains; it does not
choose which optimization techniques to combine.
Appendix [D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Core method and companion configuration map ‣ Appendix D Execution contract, algorithm and evidence attribution ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
maps each reported configuration to its actual intervention.

Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
separates harness RSI from execution within a task. The upper row shows
RSI revising the harness using training task results and complete token
cost; the lower row shows the GDR and CCS graph edits. At runtime, the
controller ingests each public receipt, updates eligibility, and either
executes a stored action or invokes the slow actor. The latter can
resolve new decisions and author another graph.

### 4.1 Executable Decision Graphs (EDG)

An EDG stores actions whose semantics and arguments slow reasoning has
already resolved. For example, a coding actor can fix a file-write
action, a make command and a pytest command. Public guards determine
whether these stored actions can execute; later receipts supply
readiness evidence without regenerating their arguments.

At slow decision $`i`$, actor $`H_{0}`$ emits the current tool action
and an EDG $`G_{i}=(V_{i},E_{i})`$, a bounded executable continuation.
Its future decision nodes are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
B_{i}=\{d_{1},\ldots,d_{m}\},\qquad d_{j}=(a_{j},\mathrm{arg}_{j},\mathrm{pred}_{j},g_{j}).
``` |  | (4) |

Here $`a_{j}`$ is the native action, $`\mathrm{arg}_{j}`$ its complete
literal arguments, $`\mathrm{pred}_{j}`$ its predecessor and
$`g_{j}:\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{public}}\rightarrow\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}`$
its public execution guard. The author fixes $`g_{j}`$ with the node;
the adapter evaluates it against subsequently observed receipts. Each
node has its own guard.

The input EDG in
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
combines reasoning, context compaction, fast decisions and tool use. For
the coding example, guards can check a missing file, available build
inputs or a successful build. Dependencies must also be complete. Edges
connect the root or an earlier node to a successor, forming an acyclic
graph. Missing or rejecting receipts prevent admission; an empty graph
returns control to the slow actor.

### 4.2 Guarded Decision Reuse (GDR)

GDR retains the graph across tool transitions. The green GDR panel shows
how a condition guard enables a reuse route around repeated reasoning.
Each observed receipt updates predecessor completion and guard truth.
Eligibility requires closed arguments needing no new semantic inference.
For node $`d_{j}`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{split}\operatorname{eligible}(d_{j},s_{t})={}&\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{pred}_{j}\text{ completed}\}\\
&\cdot\mathbf{1}\{g_{j}(s_{t})=\mathrm{true}\}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{arg}_{j}\text{ closed}\}.\end{split}
``` |  | (5) |

The eligible set is
$`\mathcal{E}(s_{t})=\{d_{j}\in B_{i}:\operatorname{eligible}(d_{j},s_{t})=1\}`$.
Guards consume observed receipts, never predicted results. Unsupported
observations, unmet dependencies or arguments requiring new inference
defer to $`H_{0}`$.

Implementation banks serialize the nodes and edges
(Appendix [C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Action adapter: CoT-authored conditional execution ‣ Appendix C Executable continuation implementation and historical adapters ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).
Literal closure is enforced by the schema and candidate-membership
checks; whether prior reasoning correctly resolved an action remains a
semantic assumption assessed through task scoring. A passing guard
proves its declared public condition, rather than general task
correctness.

A Jev-motivated typed selector returns an eligible candidate ID or
abstains, without revising arguments. A unique eligible node can execute
deterministically. Empty sets and abstention invoke the slow actor. Each
execution receipt updates the same graph.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Executable continuation implementation and historical adapters ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
specifies the public-state adapter and native integration.

### 4.3 Certified Callback Substitution (CCS)

CCS converts an admitted GDR decision into an executable replacement for
the next slow callback. It runs the exact authored action through the
original tool interface and binds the resulting receipt to the omitted
callback. At a registered original execution boundary, the parent
follows $`s_{t}\!\to\!H_{0}\!\to\!a_{t}`$. An admitted EDG decision
instead follows $`s_{t}\!\to\!d_{j}\!\to\!a_{t}`$ through the same
original tool interface. A substitution certificate binds

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{split}\kappa_{t}=(&\mathrm{graph\_hash},\mathrm{decision\_id},\mathrm{predecessor\_receipt},\\
&\mathrm{exact\_args},\mathrm{tool\_receipt},\mathrm{bypassed\_callback\_id}).\end{split}
``` |  | (6) |

The fingerprint $`\mathrm{graph\_hash}`$ identifies the authored graph
content, and $`\mathrm{decision\_id}`$ identifies its node. The
remaining fields bind the predecessor’s completion, exact executed
arguments, actual tool result and omitted callback. The orange CCS panel
depicts this substitution: a certified callback replaces the redundant
reasoning subgraph and retains its execution dependencies.

The audit matches this fingerprint and decision ID to literal arguments,
the completed predecessor’s callback and receipt, and the tool execution
receipt. It checks the registered parent boundary and requires

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
N^{\mathrm{parent}}_{\mathrm{slow},t}-N^{\mathrm{HarnessMM}}_{\mathrm{slow},t}\geq 1.
``` |  | (7) |

The parent count registers the original callback boundary. The
certificate verifies exact native execution and absence of that request,
without predicting its unobserved response or token count. Native
scoring measures task correctness; complete-task totals measure cost.
Appendix [F.3](#A6.SS3 "F.3 TRAIN substitution attribution ‣ Appendix F HumanEval mechanism attribution and causal comparison ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
records the receipt audit.

### 4.4 Complete-Task Accounting

The optimization target is complete episode cost:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C_{\mathrm{episode}}(h;x)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}(h,x)}(T_{c}^{\mathrm{in}}+T_{c}^{\mathrm{out}}).
``` |  | (8) |

The ledger charges authorship, selector inputs and outputs, added
context, remaining slow calls, fallback, recovery, finalization and
failed paid executions. Cached input remains counted. Deterministic
checks add CPU work and no actor tokens. Historical and MiMo Codex
displays retain their declared scope; complete-cost benefit claims
require all physical requests.

Development cost $`C_{\mathrm{dev}}`$ is reported separately, including
training, proposals, protected validation and rejected attempts. For
$`N`$ deployment tasks,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\overline{C}_{N}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{dev}}}{N}+\mathbb{E}_{x}[C_{\mathrm{episode}}(h;x)].
``` |  | (9) |

Shared authoring is charged exactly once to its declared development or
execution cohort. This deployment amortization is separate from reuse
within an episode. Token cost does not establish latency or energy
savings; those require separate measurements.

##### Selecting the surrounding configuration.

Training develops author prompts, context settings and adapter rules.
Disjoint validation selects among training-frozen configurations; the
selected implementation is frozen before testing. These offline choices
set the inputs and action contract of the execution controller. They
remain distinct from its online choice between an eligible stored action
and slow reasoning.
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Recorded rule-development protocol ‣ Appendix B Implementation and selection ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
gives the development protocols.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Execution contract, algorithm and evidence attribution ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
specifies the execution algorithm, assumptions and structural
invariants.

## 5 Experiments

### 5.1 Evaluation protocol

All methods use the same tasks, backbone, original tools, task limits
and scorer. All compared methods, including baselines and native
harnesses, receive token-efficiency prompts and an explicit objective to
reduce complete-task input-plus-output token consumption while
preserving task performance. Success uses the benchmark evaluation
endpoint, and token cost includes input plus output for all paid calls,
including failures. Development optimization cost is reported separately
from complete-task execution. Full-population coding comparisons use
custom 20/20/60 splits: HumanEval 33/33/98 and MBPP 85/85/257, with
deterministic rounding and fixed task IDs. TRAIN supplies revisions,
validation selects TRAIN-frozen candidates, and TEST measures the
selected configuration. The coding ablations evaluate the core execution
method; native harness pairs evaluate its integration with fixed context
and finalization settings.
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Selecting the surrounding configuration. ‣ 4.4 Complete-Task Accounting ‣ 4 HarnessMM: Reusing Decisions ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
retains the companion studies.
Appendix [D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Core method and companion configuration map ‣ Appendix D Execution contract, algorithm and evidence attribution ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
identifies their differing mechanisms, populations and cost scope.

### 5.2 Does fast execution substitute slow reasoning?

Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Does fast execution substitute slow reasoning? ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
reports model-call and substitution statistics on 98 HumanEval and 257
MBPP-sanitized test tasks. On HumanEval, the DeepSeek Harness falls from
954 to 415 paid model calls, with 147 certified callback bypasses
(1.50/task); Codex falls from 524 to 499 calls, with 18 certified
bypasses (0.18/task). On MBPP-sanitized, DeepSeek Harness falls from
1,633 to 1,088 calls, with 472 certified bypasses (1.84/task), while
success rises from 90.27% to 91.83%. The MBPP-sanitized Codex pair
records 91.83% and 90.66% success at 129.55 and 49.22 Tokens/task (k)
(Appendix [L.1](#A12.SS1 "L.1 Industrial harness comparisons ‣ Appendix L Figure 3 evaluation settings ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).
The original harnesses have zero certified bypasses. All rates use the
full task set for each method.

### 5.3 Industrial harness results

We use the official Codex and DeepSeek Harness
runtimes \[[28](#bib.bib39), [5](#bib.bib40)\], with the same pinned
backbone, original interface and scorer within each pair. HumanEval
supplies a complete held-out comparison: Codex preserves 90.82% success
with 66.72 versus 47.02 Tokens/task (k) (29.54% saving); DeepSeek
Harness improves from 71.43% to 85.71% with 96.28 versus 11.62
Tokens/task (k) (87.93% saving). Paired outcomes show five improvements
and five regressions for Codex; DeepSeek Harness has 22 improvements and
eight regressions (two-sided exact McNemar $`p=0.0161`$). These
integrated harness effects combine literal-bank reuse, context
management and finalization. Their total call-count difference is
therefore not an isolated effect of certificates; the MBPP ablations
below isolate persistence and callback retention. The MiMo-v2.6-pro
DeepSeek Harness comparison completes the same 98-task population:
baseline success is 96.94% and HarnessMM success is 97.96%, with 11.62
versus 4.40 Tokens/task (k) (62.12% saving).
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Does fast execution substitute slow reasoning? ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")(e)
reports this MiMo pair separately from the Qwen comparisons; the MiMo
Codex pair completes the same 98-task evaluation at 93.88% versus 94.90%
success. Its costs are 62.60 versus 10.09 Tokens/task (k); MiMo MBPP
Codex completes the same 257-task evaluation at 96.50% versus 97.28%
success, with 47.56 versus 11.00 Tokens/task (k); the MiMo DeepSeek
Harness pair completes the same 257-task population at 97.67% versus
98.05% success, with 6.20 versus 5.11 Tokens/task (k). Slow reasoning
authors literal action banks, and CPU receipt guards execute 480 native
substitutions
(Appendix [L.1](#A12.SS1 "L.1 Industrial harness comparisons ‣ Appendix L Figure 3 evaluation settings ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).

On MBPP, the complete Qwen-backed DeepSeek Harness comparison improves
from 90.27% to 91.83%, while Tokens/task (k) fall from 53.98 to 10.61
(80.35% saving). Slow reasoning authors executable action banks; fast
guarded execution performs 472 certified substitutions. The CoT-only
baseline reaches 93.39% at 15.04 Tokens/task (k), giving a 29.46%
HarnessMM saving.
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Does fast execution substitute slow reasoning? ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")(c)
reports this held-out pair; the independent Codex comparison records
91.83% and 90.66% success, at 129.55 and 49.22 Tokens/task (k).

Historical MBPP and GAIA2 development comparisons remain in
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Does fast execution substitute slow reasoning? ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
and
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Execution contract, algorithm and evidence attribution ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency");
they retain their development scope.

### 5.4 Companion configurations: quality and cost

Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Selecting the surrounding configuration. ‣ 4.4 Complete-Task Accounting ‣ 4 HarnessMM: Reusing Decisions ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
presents ALFWorld, SearchQA, LiveMath, AIME, Terminal-Bench 2 and GAIA2
in their original order, with No Skill, SkillOpt, AutoSaddler and
HarnessMM in each panel. The HarnessMM label identifies each study’s
selected configuration. ALFWorld varies instructions; SearchQA uses
input routing, a compact-rule draft and paid fallback; LiveMath changes
the answer-first prompt and output cap; AIME uses a compiled decision
policy with domain fallback; the archived Terminal panel uses an
instruction policy. GAIA2 combines a literal bank with context handling.
These companion studies measure their stated configurations. The MBPP
ablation supplies the direct test of EDG persistence and callback
removal
(Appendix [D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Core method and companion configuration map ‣ Appendix D Execution contract, algorithm and evidence attribution ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).

On complete SearchQA validation, HarnessMM reaches 76.76% EM at 0.99
Tokens/task (k), saving 19.08% against No Skill (paired 95% interval
$`[16.57,21.23]`$%), 38.57% against SkillOpt and 20.75% against
AutoSaddler
(Table [21](#A9.T21 "Table 21 ‣ AutoSOTA-guided all-method development comparison. ‣ I.2 Latest complete TRAIN follow-ups ‣ Appendix I Exploratory quality–cost study ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).
On all 560 AIME test questions, HarnessMM reaches 87.14% accuracy,
compared with 86.96% for No Skill, 87.86% for SkillOpt and 88.04% for
AutoSaddler. HarnessMM uses 5.90 Tokens/task (k), including shared
authorship: 14.94% below SkillOpt, 28.34% above No Skill and 20.44%
above AutoSaddler. The cost decomposition in
Table [15](#A9.T15 "Table 15 ‣ I.1 Six-benchmark Figure 2 protocols ‣ Appendix I Exploratory quality–cost study ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
shows 0.54 input, 4.28 output and 1.08 shared-author Tokens/task (k). No
Skill uses 0.22 input and 4.38 output Tokens/task (k): generated
reasoning dominates this mathematical workload. The small reduction in
HarnessMM’s execution output is outweighed by its additional input and
authorship. The comparison uses one execution per question under the
same frozen model and native scoring protocol. SkillOpt uses three
completed training rounds; AutoSaddler retains its completed four-round
policy. The separate original 18-question AIME 2025 comparison remains
in
Appendix [I.1](#A9.SS1 "I.1 Six-benchmark Figure 2 protocols ‣ Appendix I Exploratory quality–cost study ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency").
On all 480 GAIA2 test scenarios, HarnessMM reaches 43.96% success with
639.64 Tokens/task (k), compared with 42.71% and 730.22 for No Skill,
46.88% and 770.63 for SkillOpt, and 42.08% and 772.22 for AutoSaddler.
HarnessMM reduces complete actor cost by 12.41%, 17.00% and 17.17%,
respectively. The integrated harness performs 146 verified fast native
executions (1.40% of all action attempts); input accounts for 99.47% of
its actor cost
(Table [16](#A9.T16 "Table 16 ‣ GAIA2 complete comparison. ‣ I.1 Six-benchmark Figure 2 protocols ‣ Appendix I Exploratory quality–cost study ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).
It gains 1.25 percentage points over No Skill while remaining 2.92
points below SkillOpt. Each scenario runs once per method after frozen
validation selection; all unsuccessful executions remain in the quality
and cost aggregates.
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Exploratory quality–cost study ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
reports a separate quality–cost study of development candidates and
frozen GAIA2 validation results.

Under the common ALFWorld actor, HarnessMM’s frozen instructions achieve
the highest observed success and lowest model-token cost among the four
instruction policies: 66.20% at 31.12 Tokens/task (k). SkillOpt reaches
63.29% at 101.33 Tokens/task (k). The paired success difference is 2.91
points (95% floorplan-cluster interval $`[0.43,5.61]`$), with 69.29%
fewer model tokens.
Table [8](#A7.T8 "Table 8 ‣ G.1 Fresh ALFWorld instruction comparison and skill removal ‣ Appendix G Benchmark results ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
reports the four freshly executed instruction-only conditions. The
complete benchmark replay and accounting are documented in
Appendix [G.1](#A7.SS1 "G.1 Fresh ALFWorld instruction comparison and skill removal ‣ Appendix G Benchmark results ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency").

##### ALFWorld task-family instruction ablation.

Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Industrial harness results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
compares six frozen instruction conditions on the same 2,133 tasks
across seeds 9401, 9402 and 9403. HarnessMM averages 65.70% success at
31.44 Tokens/task (k). The task-family paragraph alone reaches 62.01% at
28.69 Tokens/task (k); general guidance alone reaches 49.21% at 38.94
Tokens/task (k). The family-only condition is cheaper but loses 3.69
success points. Its per-seed paired 95% floorplan-cluster intervals are
$`[2.61,6.21]`$, $`[0.48,3.76]`$ and $`[2.68,6.48]`$.

The remaining instruction conditions and per-seed paired intervals
appear in
Appendix [I.3](#A9.SS3 "I.3 Six-condition instruction ablation ‣ Appendix I Exploratory quality–cost study ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency").
All use the common actor and 50-step limit. These ablations isolate
instruction content, rather than EDG execution.

### 5.5 GDR and CCS ablation on MBPP

Our second ablation isolates GDR and CCS on
MBPP-sanitized \[[2](#bib.bib45)\] with DeepSeek Harness and a fixed
backbone.
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Industrial harness results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
compares four conditions on the same 257 tasks. Full HarnessMM reaches
93.77% success at 13.17 Tokens/task (k), versus 93.00% and 18.03 for W/o
GDR (single-use EDG). GDR reduces complete cost by 26.91%, with a
task-paired adjusted interval of \[4.01, 45.57\]%.

Full HarnessMM makes 407 certified substitutions, including repeated
bypasses in 201 graphs. W/o CCS (callbacks retained) reaches 93.39% at
16.37 Tokens/task (k), a measured 19.52% cost reduction for full
HarnessMM. Disabling EDG execution reaches 95.33% at 16.19: full
HarnessMM uses 18.62% fewer tokens but solves four fewer tasks.
Certificates verify removal; their independent benefit is not ablated.
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Second ablation: GDR and CCS ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
gives the shared execution settings, paired uncertainty and historical
comparison.

##### Evidence attribution.

The complete coding comparisons measure integrated harness quality and
cost. The single-use and retained-callback ablations directly test
persistent reuse and callback removal. Instruction-only ALFWorld
measures instruction content. Certificates establish execution and
omission, while native scoring establishes quality; no per-certificate
token value is assumed.

Figure 5: Eight training-guided harness RSI iterations on MiniWoB++.
Each comparison uses the same 32 tasks per arm, Qwen3.5-9B, full
screenshots, native rewards, 15 actions and 180 seconds per episode.
Calls/task counts physical model requests over all tasks. Tokens/task
(k) includes complete episode authorship, control, fallback and
unsuccessful calls; optimization and selection costs are separate.

### 5.6 HarnessMM harness RSI

Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Evidence attribution. ‣ 5.5 GDR and CCS ablation on MBPP ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
shows eight training-guided harness RSI iterations on the same 32
MiniWoB++ training tasks. Each pair shares the actor, author prompt,
full screenshots, coordinate compiler, guards, fallback, native scorer
and limits; single-use EDGs permit one future execution per graph, while
HarnessMM retains eligible decisions. Training feedback refines visual
grounding and screenshot context. Disjoint validation selects a frozen
configuration before testing.

Across the first eight iterations, HarnessMM success rises from 34.38%
to 90.63%, while Tokens/task (k) fall from 3.26 to 1.06 (67.43%). At the
eighth iteration, both arms solve 29 of 32 tasks; persistence saves
29.83% (1.51 versus 1.06 Tokens/task (k); paired task-bootstrap 95%
interval $`[18.84,39.00]\%`$). Calls/task fall from 1.47 to 1.03, with
16 second-and-later executions within retained graphs.

These are complete episode execution costs.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A HarnessMM visual harness RSI study ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
gives the measurements and their separate development-cost scope.

## 6 Limitations

Savings depend on provider input, cache and context accounting and on
the availability of resolved actions. New semantic decisions require
slow reasoning. Authorship, selection and recovery can outweigh avoided
calls. Public-state adapters are task specific, and small development
sets leave policy-level quality differences uncertain.

## 7 Conclusion

HarnessMM improves harness token efficiency by storing resolved
decisions, checking when they can execute and using them to replace
repeated reasoning calls. Complete HumanEval comparisons on all 98 test
tasks preserve Codex success at 90.82% with 29.54% fewer actor tokens
and improve DeepSeek Harness from 71.43% to 85.71% with 87.93% fewer
tokens. The MBPP ablation isolates persistence and callback removal;
companion studies retain their own configuration scope.

## Appendix B Implementation and selection

### B.1 QA profiles and execution

At round $`k`$, the QA harness stores profiles $`h_{\mathrm{D},k}`$
(DELETE) and $`h_{\mathrm{M},k}`$ (MODIFY). Initially, MODIFY adds five
answer-normalization rules to DELETE; the remaining four sections and
answer contract are identical. A frozen linear head selects MODIFY when
$`g(x)\geq\kappa`$, and DELETE otherwise. Its eight input-only features
are context token count, document count, question character and token
counts, question–context lexical coverage, quoted-span and relation-cue
indicators, and named-token count. The archived threshold maximizes
discovery exact matches using five-fold out-of-fold predictions, subject
to at least 8% token saving and at most 5% harm relative to SkillOpt.
Deployment reads frozen $`h_{\mathrm{D},K}`$ and $`h_{\mathrm{M},K}`$
without a router-model call, generated answers or reference labels.
Interactive tasks instead use their task-family instructions.

The full-source QA adapter retrieves original rule sentences from the
selected profile, retaining normalization and answer-format rules. It
supplies these sentences and the complete context to a draft call with a
512-token output cap. Format, source-location and explicit answer-type
checks either accept the draft unchanged or restore the complete
selected profile in a second actor call. Explicit negative/comparison
questions and multiple blanks bypass the draft. All draft and fallback
tokens are charged. Earlier compact-context and model-selected variants
have separate identities
(Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J Historical diagnostics and negative results ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).

### B.2 Recorded rule-development protocol

The historical textual pilot uses the original routed QA adapter and
32/32/32/128 source-group-disjoint tasks for training, inner validation,
meta validation and the final screen. This four-role protocol predates
the custom 20/20/60 comparisons. Training feedback contains responses,
official scores, token usage and successful cases to preserve. A fixed
compiler applies proposed edits to named rule slots after checking the
parent hash, schema, permitted fields and size constraints. It rejects
executable code, answer literals and case-specific facts. Retained rules
and answer contracts keep their source bytes; invalid proposals alias
the parent and remain charged.

A child passes the harness gate only if it changes the harness,
preserves the parent’s EM and F1 on both validation splits, uses at most
90% of Original’s inference tokens on both, and improves at least one
quality or cost endpoint over the parent. Fixed-policy RSI ranks passing
children by meta-validation EM, then F1, then lower cost. Rejection
retains the parent; the next round obtains fresh training feedback from
the retained harness. Actor weights, routing, execution code, task
interfaces, scorers and output caps stay fixed.

The restricted MetaRSI branch \[[38](#bib.bib24)\] also proposes a
strategy $`\widetilde{\pi}_{k}`$ from training feedback. Old and new
strategies receive the same parent and feedback and produce separate
children. Joint acceptance requires a changed strategy and a distinct
child that passes the harness gate, matches or exceeds the old-strategy
child’s EM and F1 at no greater cost on each validation split, and
improves at least one endpoint strictly on meta validation. Rejection
retains $`(h_{k},\pi_{k})`$, including any previously accepted strategy
change; ordinary RSI keeps $`\pi_{k}=\pi_{0}`$. Protected validation
examples and answers never enter proposal prompts. Frozen final releases
must improve EM and F1 over both Original and fixed-policy RSI, save at
least 10% of Original’s inference tokens, and use no more tokens than
fixed-policy RSI. These final-screen requirements are separate from
round acceptance.

Both branches run two rounds with two child opportunities per round and
perform no harness RSI; MetaRSI also accepts no strategy update. Six of
eight proposals fail the literal-overlap guard; the two valid three-rule
edits add 0.06 and 0.06 input Tokens/task (k) on the 32 inner-validation
tasks without improving quality or output usage. Original, fixed-policy
RSI, restricted MetaRSI and Original A/A consequently retain identical
final request bytes: each solves 78.91% of tasks (78.91 EM, 86.59 F1)
using 3.02 Tokens/task (k). Detailed acquisition costs are retained in
the external reproduction records. Unchanged deployment cost gives no
finite token break-even. The complete eight-arm screen and stage ledger
remain in generated/meta_pilot_appendix.tex and
generated/meta_optimization_costs.tex.

## Appendix C Executable continuation implementation and historical adapters

GDR reuses the authored graph across tool transitions, while CCS
executes admitted actions in place of slow callbacks and certifies their
removal. The EDG notation names the executable conditional graph
represented by the coding adapter’s serialized action bank. Bank hashes
identify the serialized graph in the archived audit. The native adapter
checks predecessor completion, literal arguments and observed public
guards before executing a node. Receipt errors, nonzero return codes,
missing dependencies and unknown or false guards return control to slow
reasoning. A unique eligible node takes a deterministic path with zero
selector tokens. Frozen adapter settings and source identities remain in
the external reproduction artifacts. The complete actor ledger includes
authorship, selection, fallback and recovery.

The complete MBPP training set (85 tasks) SDK comparison records 153
certified substitutions and 62 public-guard confirmations, with all
physical actor costs reconciled. Its policy is the historical structured
literal-bank v23 candidate. The complete selected MBPP test set (257
tasks) comparison in
Appendix [L](#A12 "Appendix L Figure 3 evaluation settings ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
evaluates the separately frozen v66 candidate. The Codex compound-bank
v10 candidate records three certified substitutions but does not pass
the broader adoption gate. The training attribution audit appears in
Appendix [F.3](#A6.SS3 "F.3 TRAIN substitution attribution ‣ Appendix F HumanEval mechanism attribution and causal comparison ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency").
The historical companion-policy vocabulary includes DELETE, BYPASS,
SUBSTITUTE, COMPACT, CACHE/REUSE, TERMINATE and COLLAPSE. It describes
the surrounding configuration search, rather than additional modules of
the EDG/GDR/CCS execution method. Recovery and finalization rules retain
their declared per-run settings.

### C.1 Execution variability and paired instruction effects

For task $`t`$, let $`x_{t}`$ be its fixed input: the task request,
supplied context, and, for a visual task, an image $`v_{t}`$. Running
the same task more than once need not produce the same answer. We write
the $`r`$-th complete execution as
$`y_{t,r}=\operatorname{Run}_{\theta}(x_{t};h,z_{t,r})`$, where
$`\operatorname{Run}_{\theta}`$ combines slow actor calls, fast
selection and tool execution operators. The input $`x_{t}`$, harness
$`h`$, and actor parameters $`\theta`$ are fixed across repeats;
$`z_{t,r}`$ captures execution conditions such as scheduling, co-batched
requests, cache state, and implementation-level variation. A client can
prescribe a concurrency and submission schedule $`s`$, but cannot
thereby fix the server’s microbatch or numerical path. Below, $`i`$
indexes decisions within one execution, and $`k`$ indexes offline
rule-development rounds.

To measure an instruction edit, we compare the original and edited
harnesses under the same prescribed schedule. Let $`m_{b}`$ be benchmark
$`b`$’s official metric for an answer or episode, and let $`y_{t}(h,s)`$
denote the response under harness $`h`$ and schedule $`s`$. The expected
score change from replacing $`h`$ with $`h^{\prime}`$ is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tau_{t}(h^{\prime},h;s)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[m_{b}(y_{t}(h^{\prime},s))-m_{b}(y_{t}(h,s))\right].
``` |  | (10) |

The expectation averages over execution conditions within that schedule.
Repeated paired executions help separate the edit’s effect from
run-to-run variation; one correct-to-wrong transition cannot do so. We
report each benchmark and quality endpoint separately.

### C.2 Inputs, outputs, and integration

HarnessMM wraps an existing decision procedure $`H_{0}`$ and preserves
its original input and output contracts. The developer supplies a task
adapter; deployment then accepts the same task request $`x`$ as the
original agent. The adapter builds public state $`s_{i}`$ from the
supplied context, current observation, and completed interaction
history. It exposes candidate decisions $`\mathcal{D}_{i}`$ and a
predicate $`c_{i}(d)`$ specifying which candidates have local support.

A decision has a type and a payload. We write an action decision as
$`\operatorname{Act}(a)`$: it executes a tool command and, if the task
continues, receives feedback for the next decision. A terminal decision
$`\operatorname{Finish}(y)`$ returns an answer and ends the task.
Fixed-context QA is the terminal-decision case of this interface. The
adapter defines the domain semantics, while the shared controller owns
support admission, candidate membership checks, commitment, and actor
fallback.

The original actor parameters, original tools, and evaluator remain
fixed. The integration requires a public-state adapter and does not
assume that arbitrary task semantics can be inferred automatically.

The offline RSI loop follows a fixed proposal strategy. The current
harness runs on training tasks; their execution feedback guides
candidate instruction edits. Disjoint validation tasks determine which
candidate to retain, and the retained harness supplies the next round’s
training feedback. The selected configuration is frozen before final
evaluation and deployment.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation and selection ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
records the development protocols.

### C.3 Shared commit-or-defer control

At each decision, the adapter prepares a candidate $`\widehat{d}_{i}`$
and its public support record. The controller applies

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
d_{i}=\begin{cases}\widehat{d}_{i},&\widehat{d}_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{i},\ c_{i}(\widehat{d}_{i})=1,\\
H_{0}(x,I_{i},s_{i}),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (11) |

Here $`I_{i}`$ is the instruction text supplied to the original actor.
An empty candidate set, unsupported state, or rejected candidate takes
the actor path. Both routes return the same typed decision to the
original interface, which commits it once. Nonterminal action feedback
updates $`s_{i+1}`$; a terminal answer ends execution without another
state update.

Candidate production and support checks have separate roles. An action
adapter can propose a tool command without calling a model; a QA adapter
first pays for an actor-generated draft. The controller records the
selected route and rejection reason, and the cost ledger includes all
model calls made by either adapter. The benchmark scorer evaluates the
selected decisions.

For action tasks, the initial actor call supplies the first transition.
Local execution then applies at every supported state. An explicit QA
bypass supplies no candidate and skips draft generation, so the
controller invokes the original answering procedure directly.

### C.4 Action adapter: CoT-authored conditional execution

The coding adapter separates constructing an action from deciding
whether the current feedback permits it. In a slow turn, the original
CoT actor \[[41](#bib.bib38)\] emits a terminal command and a bounded
action bank, the serialized EDG. Each bank entry is $`b=(\ell,p,g,a)`$:
a label $`\ell`$, a predecessor $`p`$, a condition $`g`$ on public tool
results, and literal tool arguments $`a`$. A predecessor is the current
root command or an earlier entry, so the bank defines an acyclic
execution graph. The actor declares future commands only when their
arguments are already determined; unseen data requires a new slow turn.

After a command returns, the adapter exposes entries whose predecessor
was that command. The fast selector receives the original user request,
original tool schema, declared candidates and actual public results. It
returns one candidate label or an abstention symbol. A selected label
compiles into exactly that entry’s tool command, which executes once.
The selector cannot invent commands or revise arguments. Empty banks,
unparsed results, exceeded bank limits and abstention take the original
slow path. Following each fast action, its new result determines the
next eligible entries.

The selector uses the same DeepSeek backbone as the slow actor, disables
reasoning for the selection request, and generates one control token
with model-reported log probabilities. Candidate membership and tool
arguments are checked before execution. Benchmark tests evaluate the
typed selection interface. The CoT-only control uses identical
instructions and authors the same bank format with fast selection
disabled.

The fast request retains public constraints, candidate IDs, complete
arguments and the observations needed for their guards. It omits the
full tool catalog, skill library, trajectory and slow rationale;
unsupported states defer before selection. Candidate construction, typed
selection and context compaction retain their separate mechanism
identities and complete costs. Historical adapter settings and interface
probes remain in the external reproduction artifacts.

Complete-task cost includes the slow actor’s bank authorship, every fast
input and control token, failures and slow fallbacks. Cached inputs
remain counted. The single-encoding policy supplies each decoded tool
result once to the fast selector and binds it to the original receipt
hash; the full original history remains available to slow reasoning.
Noncanonical or unsupported observations defer to CoT.
Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Industrial harness results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
distinguishes the implemented mechanism, its TRAIN comparison and final
held-out evidence.

The historical ALFWorld adapter has a different candidate producer:
handwritten state tracking records pickup, transformations and
placement, then selects the first tool action in the highest-priority
supported group. It uses neither model selection nor probability scores.
Table [8](#A7.T8 "Table 8 ‣ G.1 Fresh ALFWorld instruction comparison and skill removal ‣ Appendix G Benchmark results ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
and
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Industrial harness results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
disable that controller and compare instructions under a common actor.
These measurements are retained as instruction and historical-controller
evidence.

### C.5 Terminal adapter: answer acceptance

An answer adapter supplies a terminal candidate to the same controller.
The recorded text-QA adapter first generates a draft from the complete
source context and retrieved original rule sentences, with fixed output
budget $`L_{\mathrm{draft}}`$. Its support predicate checks the answer
format, source location, and explicit answer type. Acceptance returns
the draft unchanged. Rejection calls the original actor with the full
selected instructions. An input-only applicability check bypasses draft
generation for explicit negative/comparison questions and multiple
blanks.

The draft is a model call, and fallback is a second model call. The
original QA baseline has no separate verifier call to remove. This
adapter can change request and response lengths while adding calls on
rejected drafts; the action adapter instead avoids supported reasoning
calls. Both are measured with complete-task accounting. Stored
DELETE/MODIFY routing, source-rule retrieval, and the independently
evaluated offline rule-development loop are specified in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation and selection ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency").

## Appendix D Execution contract, algorithm and evidence attribution

HarnessMM replaces repeated reasoning calls with stored actions through
a contract between a slow author, a persistent executor and the existing
native harness boundary. A directed action graph alone is a standard
executable planning representation. Here each admitted continuation has
immutable arguments, public feedback can only change its readiness, and
the native request ledger records omission of a specified reasoning
callback. These restrictions make reuse inspectable. They do not imply
that every authored action is correct or every graph lowers cost.

### D.1 State and execution algorithm

A graph instance contains an authored root action, a finite acyclic set
of future nodes, literal native arguments, dependencies and public
guards. Runtime state contains the completed native receipts, the
remaining graph nodes and the public episode history. Graph content and
runtime state are different objects: completing a predecessor changes
the latter without rewriting the authored action.

1.  1.
    At a native decision boundary, register the parent callback and
    ingest the preceding public tool receipt. Validate its association
    with the action that produced it.
2.  2.
    Construct the eligible set from unresolved nodes whose dependencies
    are complete, public guards pass and arguments meet the adapter’s
    closure checks.
3.  3.
    If exactly one node is eligible, use the declared deterministic
    route. If several are eligible, the configured typed selector
    chooses a candidate ID or abstains. Charge any model-based selector
    input and output.
4.  4.
    On admission, execute the selected literal arguments through the
    original native interface. Record the result and compare it with the
    authored node. Emit an omission certificate only after checking
    execution and absence of the registered slow request. Mark the node
    completed and retain the unresolved remainder of the graph.
5.  5.
    On rejection, an empty set or abstention, invoke the original slow
    actor with its public task context. Record the author request and
    any fallback. A newly authored graph replaces the unresolved
    remainder; already executed receipts remain in the episode history.
6.  6.
    Continue under the common benchmark limits. A terminal answer uses
    the same commitment point and stops. The native scorer evaluates the
    complete task; the request ledger charges every paid call.

This algorithm describes the full mechanism. The coding adapter uses
literal terminal commands and observed tool results. Instruction-only
and answer-acceptance studies use different candidate producers, stated
in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Executable continuation implementation and historical adapters ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency");
they cannot be treated as independent demonstrations of persistent
coding graphs.

### D.2 Closure, guards and structural invariants

##### Literal closure and semantic closure.

Literal closure is a syntactic restriction: all executable arguments
have concrete values, with no placeholder to bind from unseen feedback.
It is checked by the action schema and candidate-membership audit.
Semantic closure is stronger: prior reasoning has determined the
action’s meaning and its future applicability is captured by the
declared guard. A concrete command can still be semantically wrong.
General semantic closure is therefore not established merely by parsing
literal arguments.

For a fixed authored decision $`d`$ and public state $`s`$, let
$`\operatorname{valid}(d,s)`$ mean that the action has its intended task
meaning at that state. Interpreting guard acceptance as semantic
permission additionally assumes

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\operatorname{eligible}(d,s)=1\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{valid}(d,s).
``` |  | (12) |

This implication depends on the adapter and the authored guard. The
implementation enforces the left-hand checks; complete native task
evaluation measures their quality consequences. There is no statewise
correctness guarantee for arbitrary tools or tasks.

##### Argument immutability.

Assume the configured adapter uses the validated graph and native
interface, the graph objects are not modified after authoring, and the
recorded receipts are faithful. A reused node executes the literal
arguments authored for that node. The typed selector returns only a node
ID; it has no argument-generation interface. Native dispatch reads the
selected stored arguments, and certificate verification compares those
values with the tool receipt. This establishes an execution invariant
under the stated assumptions, independently of task success.

##### Dependency-respecting execution.

Initially, no future node is completed. At each transition, eligibility
admits only a node whose predecessor receipts are in the completion map.
A completed node is removed from the unresolved set. Induction over
transitions therefore gives predecessor-respecting execution with at
most one dispatch per node instance. The initial acyclicity check
prevents a future node from requiring its own completion. A later author
call can create an identical graph, but it is a separate paid authoring
event.

##### Omission evidence.

A valid certificate binds the authored graph instance, selected node,
exact native arguments, predecessor receipt, tool receipt and registered
callback. The physical request ledger independently establishes absence
of the specified slow request at that boundary. This is a structural
observation about the executed route. It does not establish an identical
counterfactual trajectory, an absent call’s token quantity, or a
task-quality improvement. Comparisons on the same full task sets measure
these effects.

### D.3 Break-even analysis without counterfactual token attribution

Let $`A`$ denote additional author and selector actor tokens and $`F`$
additional fallback tokens. If $`K`$ eliminated callbacks would have
costs $`c_{1},\ldots,c_{K}`$, a same-trajectory token calculation gives
net saving only when $`\sum_{j}c_{j}>A+F`$. Under the simplifying
assumption of a common callback cost $`c>0`$, the condition is
$`K>(A+F)/c`$. This relation describes the dependence on reuse coverage;
it is not a prediction of measured saving, because the omitted calls are
not executed and the substituted trajectory can differ.

The reported estimator is instead the difference in total tokens across
all episodes for each method. Every arm uses the same independent task
membership and execution contract, and each arm’s numerator includes its
actual author, selector, slow, finalization and paid unsuccessful calls.
Shared authoring is assigned once to its declared population. Cached
provider input remains counted under the token protocol. CPU guards and
native tools affect time and behavior, but their work cannot be added to
a token total without an independently defined resource conversion.

### D.4 Novelty and closest mechanisms

ReWOO separates planning from tool observations and supports
dependency-bound evidence variables \[[43](#bib.bib49)\]; LLMCompiler
plans and dispatches tool dependencies for parallel
execution \[[19](#bib.bib50)\]. Voyager develops a library of executable
skills reused across tasks \[[40](#bib.bib19)\]. ActionEngine constructs
application-level state-machine memory, compiles task programs and
repairs execution reactively \[[52](#bib.bib54)\]. HarnessMM shares
executable planning and reuse with these approaches. Its narrower
contract stores episode-specific literal actions, lets public receipts
activate them without argument synthesis, and binds observed native
execution to a removed harness callback. We do not compare these
planning systems experimentally, so the present evidence establishes the
contract and benefits against the declared native harnesses rather than
superiority over all executable planners.

### D.5 Core method and companion configuration map

The core execution transformation has three operations: author literal
future actions, retain and activate them using public feedback, and
dispatch an eligible action while omitting its registered callback. Its
controller selects an action route. A surrounding configuration fixes
the author prompt, context serializer, native adapter and finalization
rules before the run. Those settings determine what the controller
receives; the controller does not search over them during an episode.

The reported studies use the following configurations. A row with no
persistent execution is a companion-policy study, even when its selected
policy carries the HarnessMM display label. The original run identities
and exact configuration files remain in the external reproduction
bundle.

|  Study |  Fixed surrounding intervention |  Role of executable reuse |
|----|----|----|
|  Coding harness pairs |  Literal-bank author prompt, compact public context and harness-specific finalization |  EDG/GDR/CCS enabled; complete pair measures the integrated configuration |
|  MBPP mechanism ablation |  Common author prompt, schema, public context, native tools and limits |  Change graph execution, persistence or callback retention to test the core mechanism |
|  ALFWorld |  Selected task-family and general instructions under a common actor |  Instruction-only comparison; local controller disabled |
|  SearchQA |  Frozen input-only profile routing, retrieved rule sentences, full-source draft and paid fallback |  Terminal answer acceptance; no persistent multi-action graph |
|  LiveMath |  Answer-first prompt, disabled thinking and reduced output cap |  One call per question; no callback substitution |
|  AIME |  Frozen compiled decision policy, shared authorship and domain fallback |  Measures the selected policy; execution or abstention follows its fixed applicability rules |
|  Terminal-Bench overview |  Archived AutoSaddler-derived instruction policy |  Instruction-policy snapshot; no certified EDG execution claim |
|  GAIA2 |  Frozen literal-bank authoring and public-context handling |  Integrated native execution; verified fast actions and complete costs reported together |

This map also separates cost mechanisms. Shorter prompts or context
change the tokens in a remaining call; EDG execution changes whether a
registered call occurs. The MBPP ablations keep instruction, context and
finalization settings fixed while varying graph reuse and callback
execution. No experiment in this paper trains a general policy that
dynamically composes these optimization techniques.

The token-efficiency prompt and objective apply to every comparison arm,
including No Skill, SkillOpt, AutoSaddler, the native industrial
harnesses and HarnessMM. No Skill retains the token-efficiency
instruction while omitting the added skill policy. Every arm is
instructed to reduce complete-task input-plus-output token consumption
while preserving task performance. Method-specific mechanisms and native
execution limits follow the configurations above.

### D.6 Which experiment supports which claim?

|  Evidence |  Measured intervention |  Supported interpretation |
|----|----|----|
|  HumanEval and MBPP harness pairs |  Selected HarnessMM configuration versus its original harness |  Complete task quality and actor cost for that implementation |
|  MBPP single-use graphs |  Limit each graph to one reused action |  Effect of retaining graphs across tool calls |
|  MBPP retained callbacks |  Invoke the registered slow callback while retaining graph execution |  Effect of callback removal with tasks and execution settings fixed |
|  Native execution certificates |  Match authored actions, public receipts and absent requests |  Structural execution and callback omission |
|  ALFWorld instruction comparison |  Change instructions under a common actor |  Effect of selected instruction content, not EDG substitution |
|  SearchQA and AIME studies |  Benchmark-specific selected policies and cost components |  Their declared quality–cost trade-offs, with actual phases retained |

The integrated coding results also change context management and
finalization. Total call-count reduction can therefore exceed
certificate counts; these quantities are not expected to agree. The MBPP
ablation supplies a more direct intervention test but does not isolate
the intrinsic value of recording a certificate from the value of
exclusive routing. Certificates are a measurement mechanism, and their
logging overhead is included where it makes model calls.

### D.7 Historical development evidence

Historical MBPP comparisons on 85 training tasks provide development
mechanism evidence: Codex improves from 91.76% to 94.12% at 67.21 versus
59.78 Tokens/task (k); DeepSeek Harness improves from 85.88% to 94.12%
at 15.46 Tokens/task (k) versus 11.91 Tokens/task (k). The DeepSeek
candidate records 153 certified substitutions and 62 public-guard
confirmations. Across 32 GAIA2 development scenarios, Codex improves
from 37.50% to 40.62% at 907.06 versus 825.99 Tokens/task (k), and
DeepSeek Harness improves from 40.62% to 46.88% at 891.75 Tokens/task
(k) versus 750.53 Tokens/task (k).
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Does fast execution substitute slow reasoning? ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
preserves the earlier four panels and adds two separate MiMo panels; the
appendix records their evidence phases.

The w/o skills condition averages 41.69% at 34.10 Tokens/task (k);
mismatched-family and neutral instructions of equal token length reach
48.34% at 43.28 Tokens/task (k) and 41.37% at 43.26 Tokens/task (k).
HarnessMM gains 24.00 points over the w/o skills condition while using
7.81% fewer tokens, and gains 24.33 points over neutral text with 27.33%
fewer tokens. Every action uses the common actor and the same 50-step
cap. Whiskers show the observed seed range; task identities are not
independent across repetitions.
Appendix [I.3](#A9.SS3 "I.3 Six-condition instruction ablation ‣ Appendix I Exploratory quality–cost study ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
preserves all per-seed counts, paired intervals and costs, including the
two original seed-9401 reference conditions reused exactly once. These
instruction ablations measure content effects under a common actor.

### D.8 Complete quality–cost trade-offs

Across 18 Terminal-Bench development tasks, Codex success falls from
77.78% to 55.56% while Tokens/task (k) fall from 3426.78 to 1089.95;
DeepSeek Harness falls from 55.56% to 50.00% at 1586.15 versus 1144.32
Tokens/task (k).

A complete CoT/Jev TEST comparison executes verified fast actions in
94.44% of episodes, yet costs 127.07% more than the original harness and
loses 7.29 success points. It saves only 1.04% against CoT-only, with
input tokens accounting for 98.53% of the actor ledger. The coding
control on 18 training tasks likewise records 10, 12 and 13 successes
for the original harness, CoT-only and CoT/Jev, while CoT/Jev costs
30.37% more than the original harness and 3.74% more than CoT-only.
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Industrial-harness RSI comparison ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
preserves the complete controls and their costs.

### D.9 Reproducibility and use scope

The executable adapter requires a declared native boundary, literal
action serialization, public-state guards, callback registration and
complete request logging. External reproduction artifacts retain frozen
task memberships, model and software identities, integer costs,
selection configuration and complete native outcomes. Shared optimizers
use training evidence; validation selects among frozen candidates, and
selected held-out configurations remain unchanged. Benchmarks with
historical development populations retain their actual phase rather than
being relabeled as final tests.

The controller preserves the parent’s tool permissions and action space.
It does not enlarge those permissions or establish a general safety
guarantee. Incorrect authorship, incomplete guards and changed tool
semantics can affect task quality even when the structural certificate
is valid. These cases are handled by the native evaluator and the
declared quality constraint, not by treating omission evidence as
correctness evidence.

## Appendix E Second ablation: GDR and CCS

We evaluate four conditions on the complete MBPP-sanitized release using
a custom 85/85/257 training/validation/test partition, seed 20261005.
DeepSeek Harness dsh-v0.2.0-rc.1 uses the shared backbone. All arms
share the author prompt and schema, public context, native buffered
parser, tools, decoding settings, one attempt per task, two workers per
arm, and 300-second actor/30-second verifier limits. The tool working
directory is /app; the latest actual public-check call and result remain
in public context. Authored public assertions must match the original
problem line by line. Rejected banks retain their authoring cost and
return to paid native slow reasoning. Disabled-thinking requests use the
same transport mapping across arms; task reasoning and output limits

TRAIN supplies method revisions. The sole TRAIN-qualified candidate is
frozen before validation; the predeclared aggregate capability criterion
selects it before TEST. Validation trajectories and test outcomes supply

executions. Tokens/task (k) include physical input and output from

Full HarnessMM combines GDR and CCS: GDR retains the executable graph
across tool transitions; CCS replaces slow callbacks with authored
actions and certifies their removal. W/o GDR (single-use EDG) discards
the graph after its first certified execution, preserving its author and
full authoring cost. W/o CCS (callbacks retained) retains a paid slow
callback to regenerate each selected tool action. This intervention
isolates callback substitution, not the independent benefit of
certification. Without EDG execution preserves the author and its cost
while disabling executable graph use.

### E.1 Earlier execution ablation

Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Industrial harness results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
complements the ALFWorld instruction ablation with execution
interventions on MBPP-sanitized \[[2](#bib.bib45)\]. Instructions,
authoring format, public guards and dependency checks are fixed across
the HarnessMM conditions.

#### E.1.1 Benchmark and evaluation settings

We use the complete 427-task MBPP-sanitized release with a custom
85/85/257 training/validation/test partition, seed 20261005.
Deterministic rounding implements the required 20/20/60 ratio; task
membership is disjoint and common to all arms. The parent is DeepSeek
Harness dsh-v0.2.0-rc.1 with the shared backbone. All conditions share
the public task interface, native tools, decoding settings, two workers
per arm, one execution per task and 300-second actor/30-second verifier
deadlines. Correctness evaluates every released assertion. Reference
implementations are absent from the actor workspace.

Training supplies the structured author and frozen intervention
definitions. The complete training comparison uses 85 tasks; disjoint
validation selects frozen candidates without returning trajectories or
failures to optimization. The historical evaluation uses the complete
257-task test population for every arm. Test outcomes supply no
selection or revisions; the external archive retains every arm and
execution.

#### E.1.2 Execution interventions

The original harness uses ordinary slow reasoning without EDG authoring
or fast routing. Full HarnessMM combines the structured EDG, public
eligibility checks and certified callback bypass. W/o GDR (the
single-use GDR control) preserves the author and graph capacity, but
discards unused nodes after its first certified execution. Unused
authored nodes still incur cost.

The W/o CCS condition keeps fast selection but asks the same slow actor
to regenerate exactly one tool action before execution. Changed
arguments invalidate dependent nodes; invalid regeneration returns
control to slow reasoning. A retained callback receives no substitution
certificate. Graph authorship, selector input and control, regeneration,
fallbacks and unsuccessful executions all contribute to Tokens/task (k),
normalized by the full 257-task population. Development and selection
costs remain separate from final execution.

### F.2 Additional study scope

Local decisions require a task-specific public-state adapter and support
rules. The interactive measurements use textual ALFWorld observations;
they do not establish visual-agent improvement. The ALFWorld instruction
comparison transfers archived optimized policies without rerunning their
optimizers. The custom test uses one seed and shares some floorplans
across partitions. The ALFWorld comparisons and text-QA studies use
previously exposed public data. GQA grounding and generic instructions
of equal token length both score 65% in the small visual pilot. The
separate rule-development pilot accepts no updates.

### F.4 Additional related-work and adapter context

Finally, uncertainty in model evaluation arises at multiple levels: task
sampling, prompt choice, random seeds, execution order, and
numerical/runtime behavior \[[31](#bib.bib12), [48](#bib.bib13),
[10](#bib.bib14)\]. Repeating one task characterizes its execution
distribution, with the task remaining the independent sampling unit. We
use paired source-group estimates, retain all comparison endpoints, and
separate exploratory inspection from frozen comparisons
\[[7](#bib.bib21), [32](#bib.bib23), [6](#bib.bib32)\]. Crossed and
nested dependence must be treated explicitly rather than pooling all
response cells as independent samples \[[29](#bib.bib22)\]. Efficient
serving mechanisms such as PagedAttention address execution resources
\[[20](#bib.bib20)\]; repeated-request controls characterize variability
under the chosen runtime.

The closest evaluation alternatives already address substantial parts of
our question. FormatSpread quantifies spurious prompt-format sensitivity
\[[35](#bib.bib8)\]; ProSA and POSIX examine prompt sensitivity at finer
granularity \[[54](#bib.bib9), [3](#bib.bib10)\]; PromptEval estimates
performance distributions over prompts efficiently \[[31](#bib.bib12)\].
PARC analyzes language/image transformations in vision-language models,
with certainty derived from conformal answer scores rather than repeated
execution \[[34](#bib.bib11)\]. Our comparisons combine
instruction-content controls with repeated execution and image
interventions. They examine how these sources of variation affect the
interpretation of a quality–cost comparison.

Vision-language systems combine image representations with instruction
following, and visual-programming approaches expose intermediate
operations that can be inspected or recombined \[[22](#bib.bib29),
[37](#bib.bib30)\]. These approaches motivate treating instructions as
controls over visual decisions. Balanced and compositional benchmarks,
contrastive examples, and image interventions examine complementary
aspects of this problem \[[11](#bib.bib6), [14](#bib.bib5),
[18](#bib.bib31), [26](#bib.bib7)\]. Our true-image and shuffled-image
conditions provide a within-sample diagnostic of image dependence. The
same commit-or-defer interface accepts terminal answers. A text-QA
adapter obtains an actor-generated draft, checks its source, type, and
format, and either returns it or calls the original answering procedure.
The draft and fallback are both charged. The action adapter can avoid
reasoning calls, whereas the answer adapter changes request and response
lengths. Both preserve the benchmark task interface, and complete-task
accounting covers every model call along either path.
````
