### G.5 Success-first coding search

The instruction module improves the original coding harness’s
development outcomes while reducing complete-task token use
(Table [13](#A7.T13 "Table 13 ‣ G.5 Success-first coding search ‣ Appendix G Benchmark results ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")).
The study uses all 18 TRAIN tasks in the frozen 18/18/53
Terminal-Bench 2.0 partition \[[12](#bib.bib41)\],
Codex 0.142.5 \[[28](#bib.bib39)\] and DeepSeek-flash. The original
task, common completion brief, original tools, task limits and binary
verifier are identical across conditions. The built-in-compaction
control uses Codex’s own 65,536-token trigger without reducing the
model’s context capacity.

| Condition                       | Success (%) | Tokens/task (k) |
|---------------------------------|-------------|-----------------|
| Codex parent                    | 55.56%      | 2413.56         |
| Codex + built-in compaction     | 66.67%      | 2057.72         |
| HarnessMM instruction module    | 77.78%      | 1455.83         |
| AutoSOTA-guided 32Ki compaction | 61.11%      | 1068.67         |
| AutoSOTA-guided 96Ki compaction | 61.11%      | 1176.39         |

Table 13: Complete TRAIN development comparison, one execution per task.
The instruction is selected from two TRAIN-derived candidates by
benchmark performance, then complete-task cost. All selected outputs
have executed test execution receipts; failures and compaction calls are
included in token totals. This is an instruction/context component
study, separate from the CoT/Jev decision mechanism and final held-out
evaluation. The last two rows add built-in compaction to the frozen
instruction and are rejected because their success counts fall.

Both proposed instructions solve 14 tasks. The second retains that
training success count while reducing actor tokens from 2202.94 to
1455.83 Tokens/task (k). It requires persisting every requested
artifact, checking exact paths and fields, extending working interfaces,
and recovering from observed setup errors before optional exploration.
Against the corrected original harness, it gains four successes and uses
39.68% fewer actor tokens; against built-in compaction, it gains two
successes and uses 29.25% fewer. Descriptive paired-task bootstrap
intervals for the training score differences are $`[5.56,44.44]`$ and
$`[-11.11,33.33]`$ percentage points, respectively (10,000 resamples,
seed 20260928). The selected instruction is frozen for a separate
four-arm study on 18 validation and 53 TEST tasks, with five executions
per TEST task.

Complete development acquisition costs are retained separately from
validation and deployment. The external evidence preserves exact costs,
benchmark verdicts, instructions and paired task results.

We then adapt AutoSOTA’s objective-and-reflection
workflow \[[39](#bib.bib42)\] to built-in context management. This is a
workflow adaptation, with the official CLI unused. The search holds the
instruction and original execution settings fixed, requires at least the
instruction’s 14 successes, and minimizes complete-task
input-plus-output tokens. Its first round tests a 32,768-token
compaction trigger; the frozen feedback rule chooses a shorter trigger
only if quality is preserved and tokens fall, and a longer trigger
otherwise. The 40% parent-relative saving target does not end the search
early.

The complete 32Ki round uses 1068.67 actor Tokens/task (k): 55.72% fewer
tokens than the original harness and 26.59% fewer than the instruction
module. It solves 61.11% of tasks and loses three of the instruction’s
successes, with no gains over that instruction. The paired
training-score difference is $`-16.67`$ percentage points (descriptive
95% task-bootstrap interval $`[-33.33,0.00]`$). The quality guard
rejects this candidate and evaluates the frozen 98,304-token successor.
That round also solves 61.11% of tasks, with one gain and four losses
relative to the instruction. Its paired training-score difference is
$`-16.67`$ percentage points (descriptive 95% task-bootstrap interval
$`[-38.89,5.56]`$). It uses 1176.39 actor Tokens/task (k), 51.26% fewer
than the original harness and 19.20% fewer than the instruction, but
10.08% more than the 32Ki round. Both candidates therefore fail the
77.78% quality requirement and remain ineligible for protected
validation. The two completed rounds add 2245.06 Tokens/task (k) to
development expenditure.
Table [13](#A7.T13 "Table 13 ‣ G.5 Success-first coding search ‣ Appendix G Benchmark results ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")

## Appendix H Industrial-harness RSI comparison

Codex 0.142.5 uses the Responses API; DeepSeek Harness dsh-v0.2.0-rc.1
uses the Messages API. Both use DeepSeek-flash, byte-preserving
metering, the ARE 1.1.0 scorer and the custom GAIA2-mini 32/32/96 split
(seed 20260928). Each descendant is paired with its own industrial seed.

Each search makes two sparse-instruction proposals on all 32 training
scenarios. The second receives the first candidate’s training feedback.
A grouped cross-fitted router admits only positive supported advantage;
protected validation selects among admitted candidates and the seed.
Codex applies residual instructions through task-local AGENTS.md;
DeepSeek uses an additive system-prompt section. Original execution
loops, tools, model and task limits stay fixed. Policy, adapter, scorer
and source hashes freeze before testing; validation failures and test
outcomes never enter the proposer.

Both searches reject their two candidates and retain the seed. The
complete tests compare independent executions of each unchanged harness:
Codex records 10.42% versus 9.03% success; DeepSeek records 8.68% versus
7.64%. Their paired differences are $`-1.39`$ and $`-1.04`$ points, with
95% scenario-cluster intervals $`[-3.47,0.35]`$ and $`[-3.47,1.04]`$,
respectively (10,000 resamples, seed 20260928).

Independent benchmark replay also reproduces all 2,010 archived outcomes
and provider-token totals for the full controller, skills-only actor and
three prompt controls. The historical 100% result includes handwritten
task rules and does not measure an RSI optimization gain.

### J.2 Archived action-controller comparisons

The complete official134 replication uses all valid_unseen tasks, seeds
9401–9403 and a common 50-step limit. The support-first handwritten
controller solves 100.00% at each seed, versus 67.16%, 67.91% and 69.40%
for its skills-only actor. The stall-gated predecessor solves 97.76%,
99.25% and 97.76%; removing its progress filter gives 35.07%, 32.84% and
34.33%. Removing its skill text gives 97.76%, 97.01% and 97.76%. These
interventions belong to the predecessor, separate from the
instruction-only ablation in
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Industrial harness results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency").
All ten configurations and their per-seed costs remain in
generated/jev_mechanism_confirmation.tex. The 134 tasks, not the 402
repeated executions, are the independent units.

On the separate custom test set (2133, tasks) support-first execution
solves 95.08% of tasks at 1.00 Tokens/task (k), versus 92.55% at 9.91
for stall gating. The paired 80 gains and 26 losses give a 2.53-point
difference (95% floorplan-cluster interval $`[0.98,4.07]`$) and 89.89%
token saving. Both use the same instructions, selector and 50-step cap.
This compares historical controller configurations. The earlier
development set (60 tasks) selection used opened tasks and unequal
historical limits; it supplies no additional held-out evidence.

### J.3 Recorded execution examples

The archived stall-gated traces illustrate both progress and failure. In
the heating example, the controller picks up egg 3 at step 13, heats it
at 15, and places it in the fridge at 17. Heating feedback updates the
tracked state, excluding the otherwise legal cooling action. The episode
succeeds in 18 steps with seven model calls and 8.17 Tokens/task (k) for
that single episode. In the two-book example, the placement ledger
distinguishes the first completed book from the remaining target; the
run succeeds in 22 steps with 11 calls and 9.96 Tokens/task (k). In the
heated-cup failure, supported exploration reaches the still-closed
fridge at the final allowed step, 48, without finding and heating the
cup. Local support does not guarantee timely task completion. These are
the lexicographically first recorded success/failure examples in their
categories, bound in evidence/jev_execution_examples.json; they are
illustrative, not additional evaluation samples.

### J.4 Compression and transfer failures

Earlier SearchQA studies use 5,000 opened training-source questions. The
9B compact-context deterministic adapter reaches 70.54 EM at 1.90
Tokens/task (k) versus 75.46 at 3.00 for fresh original HarnessMM:
36.71% fewer tokens with a 4.92-point loss. Model-selected recovery
reaches 73.42 at 3.02 Tokens/task (k). The later evaluations retain full
source context.

The separate studies with the same backbone also fail their quality
targets. Model-based typed checks reach 72.12 EM at 4.08 Tokens/task (k)
versus 73.32 at 3.00 Tokens/task (k) for original HarnessMM, falling
back on 87.80% of tasks. Probability-only full/compact source selection
reaches 44.16/45.06 EM. Adding 96 CoT tokens gives 29.00 versus 27.06
for its fresh zero-CoT control; restoring a short evidence sentence
gives 35.10 versus 19.98 for its label-alias control. The initial
evidence-generation attempt was inactive and scored 20.10. Source-rule
typed recovery reaches 69.72 versus 72.08 for fresh original HarnessMM,
saving only 10.50% against its 30% target. Each study retains its own
model, request template, complete controls and accounting in the source
bundle; none replaces the later full-source result.

Spreadsheet’s opened LOGO267 replay gives 4.12% at 48.36 Tokens/task (k)
for archived No Skill, 3.00% at 51.58 Tokens/task (k) for SkillOpt,
2.25% at 47.77 Tokens/task (k) for AutoSaddler, and 3.00% at 11.78
Tokens/task (k) for HarnessMM. The last three use fresh executions;
HarnessMM retains 170 repair/abstention routes and 97 No-Skill routes
chosen post hoc by workbook group. Its separate seven-condition test on
200 opened tasks gives deterministic recovery 2.50%, matching original
HarnessMM at 25.06% lower cost, but below No Skill and AutoSaddler at
3.50%. Its 97-task state-controller study solves 0.00% versus the
parent’s 1.03% while increasing cost. The earlier Terminal-Bench subset
gives HarnessMM 8.33% versus 25.00% for each baseline; the visual-web
subset gives 25.00% versus 33.33% for No Skill and SkillOpt.

The AIME draft-isolation diagnostic scores 70.00% versus 80.00% for both
visible-draft verification and the shared drafts. GAIA2’s
feedback-consistent controller reduces repeated restorations from 64 to
3 and Tokens/task (k) from 929.89 to 838.67, but scores 83.33% versus
90.00% for its original harness evaluated on the same development tasks
in a new run. The older budget-limited GAIA2 run and email-pagination
activation diagnostic have incomplete outcomes across methods; neither
supports a quality or cost comparison.

### J.5 Instruction-content and visual diagnostics

The five-module response study evaluates all 32 masks, ten equal-length
body controls and Original A/A on 256 discovery tasks and 257
held-out-stage tasks in 256 source groups. The full harness solves
84.82%; the discovery-selected normalization/answer-type mask solves
84.44% at 23.91% lower cost. No module passes the primary familywise
criterion, and no average main effect or pair interaction passes the
Holm-corrected secondary tests. Nineteen tasks vary in EM across masks;
the outcome-selected oracle reaches 86.77% and is not a deployable
selector.

The targeted replication retains those 19 tasks, two F1-only cases and
32 stable controls, with six arms in eight blocks (four serial, four
16-concurrent). Eighteen of the 19 EM effects retain their mean
direction, and 17 retain a nonzero sign in every block; both F1-only
effects persist. Stable controls have zero EM edge effects, while
Original A/A changes EM on two variable tasks. These are conditional,
outcome-selected effects; 13 of the 19 nominated modules concern
normalization. All retained module bytes, ordering and answer contracts
are unchanged, and generic/unrelated controls exactly match complete
model input token counts.

The GQA pilot evaluates 40 balanced questions in 19 image groups, plus
88 entailment-support questions, with three repeats. True-image accuracy
is 62.50% for the base and 65.00% for both grounding and generic
instructions of equal token length; shuffled-image accuracy is 35.00%,
33.33% and 35.00%, respectively. Grounding and generic correctness
coincide on every balanced task. Their true-minus-shuffled interaction
is 1.67 points, with a descriptive image-cluster interval of
$`[-2.44,7.69]`$. Images use 448-by-448 padded renderings with 196 model
image tokens. The 2,304 benchmark requests consume 0.27 Tokens/task (k);
admission adds 500. Model image tokens and the unchanged publisher
scorer were replayed independently \[[14](#bib.bib5)\].

Two later feasibility studies also stop before final evaluation. Text
calibration evaluates 512 groups over three repeats after training on
2,048 groups; all four adaptive thresholds fail the joint gate. The
least restrictive saves 4.3734% while lowering EM and F1; the
quality-preserving three-short-route policy saves only 0.1483%. For the
MMMU instruction library, 270 calls on 90 training questions consume
0.65 Tokens/task (k), including 0.51 input-image/task (k). Even zero
output permits only 0.366% saving, below the 10% target. This is a
cost-feasibility bound; task accuracy was not measured. The completed
gate records remain in generated/token_efficiency_protocol.tex;
unexecuted plans are omitted from the paper.

## Appendix K Reproducibility

generated/CLAIM_EVIDENCE.json binds reported values to source artifacts,
model identities and evaluation scope. Raw remote-run records retain
frozen policies and partitions, model/tokenizer revisions, physical GPU
assignments, seeds, packages, requests, outputs and usage, including
failures. Audits reconstruct original API requests, scores and tokens.
Historical tables retain their original cohorts, method identities and
costs in generated/.

In 17 audited GAIA2 worker launches, startup PYTHONHASHSEED was not
recorded. ARE 1.1.0 uses Python’s salted hash for some receipt ordering
and app-RNG seeds; a fixed model-server seed does not establish
identical tool trajectories. OS-generated UUIDs and measured simulation
timing remain variable. The source audit is bound in
evidence/gaia2_native_seed_audit_20261002.json.

The primary source bindings are evidence/alfworld_fresh226_panel.json,
evidence/figure1_bdf.json, evidence/aime202060_complete.json,
evidence/industrial_harness_panel.json,
evidence/industrial_harness_deepseek_test.json and
evidence/figure1_df_current.json.
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Exploratory quality–cost study ‣ HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvementfor Harness Token Efficiency")
binds the quality–cost follow-up. Exact split IDs accompany the 20/20/60
protocol; benchmark licenses and release conditions apply.

Token totals include all input/output, truncations and fallback. Search,
rejected proposals, validation, judges and shared acquisition are
separate; inherited calls are charged once. Finite break-even requires
measured development cost and positive per-task savings. Unknown
historical costs stay unknown. Runs have no cumulative token stop; model
capacities and benchmark task limits remain. In the paper directory,
bash build.sh renders and compiles saved results without model or
benchmark calls; template-dependency.json pins the CVPR and bibliography
styles.
